prompt:
You are a junior associate at a litigation firm representing a client facing a similar religious exemption claim against a large employer. The senior partner has asked you to draft a memorandum analyzing the legal standards applied in Gardner-Alfred v. Federal Reserve Bank of New York, 143 F.4th 51 (2d Cir. 2025), to advise on the viability of your client's claim.

The attached document is the Second Circuit's opinion in Gardner-Alfred v. Federal Reserve Bank of New York (143 F.4th 51). The case involves two plaintiffs, Lori Gardner-Alfred and Jeanette Diaz, who sought religious exemptions from their employer's mandatory Covid-19 vaccination policy. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York denied their requests and terminated them. The district court granted summary judgment for the Federal Reserve on all claims and imposed discovery sanctions. The Second Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Gardner-Alfred but vacated and remanded for Diaz, finding disputed factual issues regarding her sincerely held religious beliefs.

Your task is to prepare a legal memorandum for the senior partner that:
1. Identifies and analyzes the key legal standards from Gardner-Alfred relevant to religious exemption claims under RFRA, the Free Exercise Clause, and Title VII.
2. Compares how the court evaluated the sincerity of the plaintiffs' religious beliefs and why the outcomes differed for Gardner-Alfred and Diaz.
3. Explains the court's analysis of whether the vaccination policy substantially burdened religious exercise and whether it satisfied strict scrutiny (for RFRA/Free Exercise) or the undue hardship standard (for Title VII).
4. Discusses the procedural history and discovery sanctions, focusing on how they affected the case.
5. Provides practical advice for a client in a similar position, based on the court's reasoning.

Your memorandum should be structured with clear headings, cite specific parts of the opinion, and be no longer than 8 pages. Use standard legal citation format. The memorandum should be a Word document (.docx) with a header including 'To:', 'From:', 'Date:', and 'Re:' lines. File name should be 'Legal Memo - Gardner-Alfred Analysis.docx'.

sections.heading: Introduction and Summary
required_content: Identify the case and citation
Summarize the Second Circuit's holding regarding Gardner-Alfred and Diaz
State the memorandum's purpose
paragraphs: This memorandum analyzes the legal standards applied by the Second Circuit in Gardner-Alfred v. Federal Reserve Bank of New York, 143 F.4th 51 (2d Cir. 2025), regarding religious exemption claims from employer vaccination mandates. The case involved plaintiffs Lori Gardner-Alfred and Jeanette Diaz, employees at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, who sought religious exemptions from a policy requiring Covid-19 vaccination. The Federal Reserve denied their requests and ultimately terminated them for noncompliance. The district court granted summary judgment for the Federal Reserve on all federal claims and imposed discovery sanctions. On appeal, the Second Circuit affirmed summary judgment against Gardner-Alfred but vacated and remanded the judgment against Diaz, finding disputed issues of material fact concerning the sincerity of her religious beliefs.

The opinion provides important guidance on evaluating religious exemption claims under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA), the Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment, and Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. This memorandum will analyze the court's legal standards, compare the outcomes for the two plaintiffs, and offer practical advice for clients facing similar situations.

sections.heading: Factual Background
required_content: Describe the employer and employees' positions
Explain the vaccination policy and exemption process
Detail the timeline of exemption requests, accommodations, and termination
Note the filing and procedural history up to summary judgment
paragraphs: Lori Gardner-Alfred and Jeanette Diaz were executive assistants to C-suite officers at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York when the Covid-19 pandemic began. In March 2020, the Federal Reserve shifted most employees, including Gardner-Alfred and Diaz, to remote work. In summer 2021, as part of a phased return to the office, the Federal Reserve adopted a vaccination policy requiring that 'every individual employed by the [Federal Reserve] must be fully vaccinated against COVID-19' as a condition of employment, with accommodations available for those with 'a sincerely held religious belief that precludes receiving the COVID-19 vaccine.'

Gardner-Alfred and Diaz applied for religious exemptions on August 9, 2021, and September 1, 2021, respectively. The Federal Reserve granted them both temporary accommodations until November 30, 2021. On November 29, 2021, the Federal Reserve denied permanent accommodations, stating their temporary accommodations would expire on January 7, 2022, and that they needed to be vaccinated by December 26, 2021. Neither complied, and both were terminated on March 14, 2022.

Prior to termination, they filed suit in New York Supreme Court seeking to enjoin their firing. The case was removed to the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York. After discovery, the district court granted summary judgment for the Federal Reserve on all federal claims and imposed discovery sanctions. The state and city claims had been previously dismissed on a motion to dismiss.

sections.heading: Legal Standards for Religious Exemption Claims
required_content: Explain RFRA's substantial burden and strict scrutiny framework
Explain Free Exercise Clause analysis under Employment Division v. Smith
Explain Title VII's reasonable accommodation and undue hardship standard
Discuss the role of sincerity in each framework
paragraphs: The Second Circuit evaluated the plaintiffs' claims under three distinct legal frameworks: RFRA, the Free Exercise Clause, and Title VII. Under RFRA, the government 'shall not substantially burden a person's exercise of religion' unless it demonstrates that the burden '(1) is in furtherance of a compelling governmental interest; and (2) is the least restrictive means of furthering that compelling governmental interest.' This imposes a strict scrutiny standard.

The Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment, as interpreted in Employment Division v. Smith, 494 U.S. 872 (1990), generally does not require religious exemptions from neutral, generally applicable laws. However, the Supreme Court's decision in Fulton v. City of Philadelphia, 593 U.S. 567 (2021), and related cases have complicated this analysis.

Under Title VII, an employer must reasonably accommodate an employee's sincerely held religious beliefs unless doing so would impose an 'undue hardship on the conduct of the employer's business.' This is a less demanding standard than strict scrutiny, but still requires an individualized assessment.

A critical threshold question in all three frameworks is whether the claimant holds 'sincerely held religious beliefs.' Courts examine the sincerity, not the truth or correctness, of professed beliefs. The Gardner-Alfred opinion demonstrates how factual disputes over sincerity can preclude summary judgment, as seen in Diaz's case.

sections.heading: Analysis of Sincerity: Gardner-Alfred vs. Diaz
required_content: Explain why the court found no dispute of fact for Gardner-Alfred
Explain why the court found disputed facts for Diaz
Discuss the evidence and reasoning for each plaintiff
paragraphs: The district court concluded there was 'no genuine dispute of fact that Gardner-Alfred and Diaz did not have sincerely held religious objections to the Federal Reserve's vaccination policy.' However, the Second Circuit disagreed with this conclusion as to Diaz. The opinion indicates that the sincerity inquiry is factual and context-dependent.

For Gardner-Alfred, the court found no basis to disturb the summary judgment. The opinion implies that her stated objections were not sufficiently supported by evidence to create a genuine dispute. The record apparently lacked evidence linking her objections to religious beliefs rather than secular concerns.

For Diaz, however, the Second Circuit found 'disputed issues of material fact about whether Diaz's sincerely held religious beliefs conflict with the Federal Reserve's vaccination policy.' This indicates that Diaz presented more substantial evidence—perhaps consistent statements, religious affiliations, or specific doctrinal objections—that, taken in the light most favorable to her, could lead a reasonable jury to conclude her beliefs were sincere. The court remanded her claims for trial on this issue.

The contrasting outcomes highlight that sincerity is not presumed; it must be supported by evidence. Plaintiffs seeking religious exemptions should be prepared to demonstrate a consistent, historically rooted connection between their beliefs and the specific practice at issue.

sections.heading: Substantial Burden and Compelling Interest/Undue Hardship Analysis
required_content: Discuss the court's analysis of whether the policy substantially burdened religious exercise
Explain the compelling interest/strict scrutiny analysis under RFRA
Explain the undue hardship analysis under Title VII
Note any distinctions between the standards
paragraphs: The opinion indicates that the district court also analyzed whether the vaccination policy conflicted with Diaz's professed religious beliefs—a separate question from sincerity. This goes to whether there is a substantial burden under RFRA or a conflict requiring accommodation under Title VII.

If a plaintiff's beliefs are sincere but do not actually conflict with the policy, then no burden exists. The Second Circuit's remand suggests that for Diaz, this conflict was also genuinely disputed. For Gardner-Alfred, the lack of sincerity likely mooted this analysis.

Under RFRA, if a substantial burden is found, the burden shifts to the employer to demonstrate that the policy serves a compelling governmental interest and is the least restrictive means. The Federal Reserve would likely argue that workplace safety and public health are compelling interests, especially in a financial institution with critical functions.

Under Title VII, the standard is 'undue hardship,' defined as more than a de minimis cost. The Supreme Court in Groff v. DeJoy, 600 U.S. 447 (2023), recently clarified this standard, but the Gardner-Alfred opinion does not discuss it in detail. The district court's analysis likely focused on the Federal Reserve's operational needs and the difficulty of accommodating unvaccinated employees in a shared workplace.

The discovery sanctions imposed by the district court—adverse inference instructions and attorneys' fees—also weighed against the plaintiffs. While the Second Circuit affirmed the sanctions, finding no abuse of discretion, the sanctions likely undermined the plaintiffs' ability to prove their case at summary judgment.

sections.heading: Procedural History and Discovery Sanctions
required_content: Describe the discovery misconduct
Explain the sanctions imposed
Discuss the appellate review standard for sanctions
Note the impact on the case
paragraphs: The district court found that Gardner-Alfred and Diaz 'repeatedly failed to comply with their discovery obligations, violated the court's discovery orders, and withheld relevant, potentially damaging documents.' The court concluded their conduct was 'willful' and 'in bad faith.' Sanctions were imposed under Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 16(f), 37(b), 37(c), and 26(g).

The sanctions included: (1) adverse inference instructions against the plaintiffs, and (2) an award of reasonable attorneys' fees and expenses incurred by the Federal Reserve in connection with the sanctions motion, correspondence regarding discovery deficiencies, and a related motion. The district court applied the 'least harsh sanction that can provide an adequate remedy' standard.

The Second Circuit reviewed the sanctions for abuse of discretion and found none. The plaintiffs did not challenge the factual findings of misconduct on appeal, focusing instead on the legal sufficiency of the sanctions.

Discovery sanctions can severely impact a case. Adverse inferences allow the jury to assume that withheld documents would have been unfavorable to the sanctioned party. Here, the sanctions likely made it harder for the plaintiffs to demonstrate sincerity and conflict at summary judgment, as the court could draw negative inferences from their discovery behavior.

sections.heading: Practical Advice for Clients
required_content: Recommend consistent documentation of religious beliefs
Advise on the importance of sincerity evidence
Warn about discovery obligations
Suggest early legal consultation
paragraphs: Based on the Gardner-Alfred opinion, clients seeking religious exemptions from employer mandates should take several steps to strengthen their position. First, they should document their religious beliefs early and consistently. This includes written statements, affiliation with religious organizations, and any communications with religious leaders. The court's focus on sincerity means that contemporaneous evidence is crucial.

Second, clients should ensure their professed beliefs directly conflict with the policy. A generalized objection is insufficient; the belief must be specifically tied to the practice at issue. For vaccination mandates, this might involve showing a religious tenet against receiving certain medical treatments.

Third, clients must strictly comply with all discovery obligations. The sanctions in Gardner-Alfred—adverse inferences and fee awards—demonstrate that misconduct can be fatal to a claim. Even if the underlying claim has merit, discovery violations can undermine it at summary judgment.

Finally, clients should consult legal counsel early. The procedural history of this case, including the motion to dismiss and the sanctions motion, shows that religious exemption claims involve complex procedural and substantive hurdles. Early guidance can help avoid pitfalls and preserve claims.

sections.heading: Conclusion
required_content: Summarize key takeaways
Restate the significance of the case
paragraphs: The Gardner-Alfred opinion underscores that religious exemption claims are intensely fact-specific. The sincerity of religious beliefs is a factual question that can preclude summary judgment if adequately supported, as shown by Diaz's case. However, claims without sufficient evidence of sincerity or conflict will fail, as with Gardner-Alfred.

The case also highlights the procedural pitfalls of discovery misconduct, which can irremediably damage even potentially meritorious claims. For clients in similar situations, careful documentation, consistent testimony, and strict compliance with litigation obligations are essential to preserving their religious liberty claims.

# Seed Material: Gardner-Alfred v. Federal Reserve Bank of New York
Source: courtlistener
Identifier: cluster:10621884

Case Name: Gardner-Alfred v. Federal Reserve Bank of New York
Citation: 143 F.4th 51
Court: ca2
Date Filed: 2025-07-02
Judges: None

## Opinion Text
23-7544 Gardner-Alfred v. Federal Reserve Bank of New York UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE SECOND CIRCUIT August Term, 2024 Argued: December 4, 2024 Decided: July 2, 2025 Docket No. 23-7544-cv LORI GARDNER-ALFRED, JEANETTE DIAZ, Plaintiffs-Appellants, — v. — FEDERAL RESERVE BANK OF NEW YORK, Defendant-Appellee. B e f o r e: LYNCH, NARDINI, and LEE, Circuit Judges. __________________ In 2021, defendant-appellee the Federal Reserve Bank of New York (the “Federal Reserve”) adopted a policy requiring all employees to be vaccinated against Covid-19 unless they were granted a religious or medical exemption. Plaintiffs-appellants Lori Gardner-Alfred and Jeanette Diaz, employees at the Federal Reserve, applied for religious exemptions, asserting that receiving a Covid-19 vaccine was against their religious beliefs. The Federal Reserve denied their requests and ultimately fired them for violating the vaccination policy. Gardner-Alfred and Diaz assert that the Federal Reserve’s actions impinged on their religious liberties guaranteed by the Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment and various federal statutes. Following discovery, the district court granted the Federal Reserve’s motion for summary judgment on all of Gardner-Alfred’s and Diaz’s federal claims, concluding that there was no genuine dispute of fact that Gardner-Alfred and Diaz did not have sincerely held religious objections to the Federal Reserve’s vaccination policy, and that the vaccination policy did not conflict with Diaz’s professed religious beliefs. We conclude that the district court (Liman, J.) correctly granted summary judgment on Gardner-Alfred’s claims. We find, however, that disputed issues of material fact preclude summary judgment on Diaz’s claims. We also conclude that the district court did not abuse its discretion in granting the Federal Reserve’s motion for discovery sanctions, locating no clear error in the district court’s findings that Gardner-Alfred and Diaz repeatedly neglected their discovery obligations, withheld relevant documents, and flouted the district court’s orders. We therefore AFFIRM in part and VACATE in part the judgment of the district court, and REMAND the case for further proceedings. STEVEN M. WARSHAWSKY, The Warshawsky Law Firm, Mt. Kisco, NY (John G. Balestriere, Michael J. Weiner, Balestriere Fariello, New York, NY on the briefs), for Plaintiffs-Appellants. ALEX LEONARD (Daphne Ha, Michele Kalstein on the brief), Federal Reserve Bank of New York, New York, NY for Defendant- Appellee. 2 GERARD E. LYNCH, Circuit Judge: Defendant-appellee the Federal Reserve Bank of New York (the “Federal Reserve”) declined the requests of plaintiffs-appellants Lori Gardner-Alfred and Jeanette Diaz for a religious exemption from a policy that required all Federal Reserve employees to be fully vaccinated against Covid-19. The Federal Reserve then fired Gardner-Alfred and Diaz when they failed to comply with that vaccination policy. Gardner-Alfred and Diaz sued, claiming that the Federal Reserve’s actions infringed upon their religious liberties in violation of, inter alia, the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, the Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment, and Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. The district court (Lewis J. Liman, J.) granted summary judgment to the Federal Reserve on Gardner-Alfred’s and Diaz’s claims. In addition, the district court found that, while litigating their claims, Gardner-Alfred and Diaz both engaged in discovery misconduct, and on motion of the Federal Reserve, imposed sanctions in the form of adverse inference instructions and an award of attorneys’ fees and expenses occasioned by that misconduct. On appeal, Gardner- Alfred and Diaz challenge the district court’s imposition of discovery sanctions and grant of summary judgment against them. 3 We conclude that the district court did not abuse its discretion by imposing sanctions and that the district court properly granted summary judgment on Gardner-Alfred’s claims. We also conclude, however, that disputed issues of material fact about whether Diaz’s sincerely held religious beliefs conflict with the Federal Reserve’s vaccination policy preclude summary judgment against Diaz. Accordingly, we AFFIRM in part and VACATE in part the judgment of the district court, and REMAND the case for further proceedings. BACKGROUND Gardner-Alfred and Diaz were executive assistants to C-suite officers at the Federal Reserve when the Covid-19 pandemic began. Like many other employers, the Federal Reserve responded to the pandemic by shifting most of its employees, including Gardner-Alfred and Diaz, to remote work starting in March of 2020. That policy continued until, in the summer of 2021, the Federal Reserve announced its intention to begin “a phased return to the office after Labor Day,” which required employees to return to work in person several days a week. App’x 893. As part of that transition, the Federal Reserve adopted a vaccination policy, which provided that “[a]s a condition of employment, every individual 4 employed by the [Federal Reserve] must be fully vaccinated against COVID-19, as defined in applicable public health guidance, and receive a booster shot within thirty (30) days of becoming eligible to do so, unless they receive an accommodation related to this requirement.” Id. 56. As relevant here, employees could apply for an exemption from the policy based on “a sincerely held religious belief that precludes receiving the COVID-19 vaccine” by submitting “a religious accommodation request form” with a “clear[]” explanation as to “why receiving the COVID-19 vaccination would be contrary to their religious beliefs.” Id. 57. Gardner-Alfred and Diaz sought religious exemptions from the vaccination policy on August 9, 2021 and September 1, 2021, respectively. The Federal Reserve granted them both “temporary accommodation[s]” from the vaccination policy until November 30, 2021. Id. 86, 1092. On November 29, however, the Federal Reserve decided not to grant Gardner-Alfred and Diaz permanent religious accommodations, indicated that their temporary accommodations would expire on January 7, 2022, and informed them that they would need to be vaccinated by December 26, 2021 to comply with the vaccination policy. Ultimately, Gardner-Alfred and Diaz did not get vaccinated and, as a result, they were fired on March 14, 2022. 5 I. Procedural History A. Early Stages of the Lawsuit Prior to their termination, Gardner-Alfred and Diaz filed this lawsuit in the Supreme Court of New York, seeking to enjoin the Federal Reserve from firing them for their refusal to comply with the vaccination policy.1 The Federal Reserve timely removed the case to the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York. Gardner-Alfred and Diaz then filed an amended complaint, the operative complaint for purposes of this appeal, alleging that the Federal Reserve’s actions violated the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (“RFRA”), the Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment, Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, New York State’s Human Rights Law, and New York City’s Human Rights Law. On the Federal Reserve’s motion to dismiss the amended complaint, the district court dismissed the claims under New York State’s and New York City’s Human 1 Although the state court issued a temporary restraining order, prohibiting the Federal Reserve from firing Gardner-Alfred and Diaz, after the case was removed to federal court, the district court dissolved the temporary restraining order because Gardner-Alfred and Diaz failed to “satisfy the requirements of Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 65” and failed to “carr[y] their burden of justifying continuing injunctive relief.” Gardner-Alfred v. Federal Reserve Bank of New York, No. 22-cv-1585, 2022 WL 748249, at *3–4 (S.D.N.Y. Mar. 11, 2022). 6 Rights Laws but permitted the federal claims to proceed. See Gardner-Alfred v. Federal Reserve Bank of New York, 651 F. Supp. 3d 695, 698 (S.D.N.Y. 2023). B. Discovery After almost a year of discovery, the Federal Reserve moved for discovery sanctions, alleging that Gardner-Alfred and Diaz were flouting their discovery obligations under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and the district court’s discovery orders. After full briefing and a hearing, the district court found that Gardner-Alfred and Diaz had repeatedly failed to comply with their discovery obligations, violated the court’s discovery orders, and withheld relevant, potentially damaging documents.2 Based on the nature of Gardner-Alfred’s and Diaz’s non-compliance with their discovery obligations and the court’s orders, the district court concluded that Gardner-Alfred and Diaz acted “willful[ly]” and “in bad faith” and that their misconduct warranted the imposition of sanctions under Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 16(f), 37(b), and 37(c). Gardner-Alfred v. Federal Reserve Bank of New York, No. 22-cv-1585, 2023 WL 3495091, at *8–14 (S.D.N.Y. May 17, 2023). In addition, the district court found that sanctions under Federal Rule of Civil 2 Gardner-Alfred and Diaz do not challenge those factual findings on appeal. 7 Procedure 26(g) were warranted against Diaz, Gardner-Alfred, and their counsel because they had falsely represented on numerous occasions that they had produced all responsive documents. Id. at *14–16.3 Having concluded that sanctions were in order, the district court turned to determining “the least harsh sanction that can provide an adequate remedy” for such blatant misconduct. Id. at *16 (quotation marks omitted). First, the district court concluded that the Federal Reserve was entitled to reasonable expenses and attorneys’ fees incurred in connection with (1) the [sanctions] motion, (2) call and email correspondence with opposing counsel from March 21 to the present date regarding [Gardner-Alfred’s and Diaz’s] discovery deficiencies; as well as (3) expenses incurred in connection with their February 27 motion

We find, however, that disputed issues of material fact preclude summary judgment on Diaz’s claims. We also conclude that the district court did not abuse its discretion in granting the Federal Reserve’s motion for discovery sanctions, locating no clear error in the district court’s findings that Gardner-Alfred and Diaz repeatedly neglected their discovery obligations, withheld relevant documents, and flouted the district court’s orders. We therefore AFFIRM in part and VACATE in part the judgment of the district court, and REMAND the case for further proceedings. STEVEN M. WARSHAWSKY, The Warshawsky Law Firm, Mt. Kisco, NY (John G. Balestriere, Michael J. Weiner, Balestriere Fariello, New York, NY on the briefs), for Plaintiffs-Appellants. ALEX LEONARD (Daphne Ha, Michele Kalstein on the brief), Federal Reserve Bank of New York, New York, NY for Defendant- Appellee. 2 GERARD E. LYNCH, Circuit Judge: Defendant-appellee the Federal Reserve Bank of New York (the “Federal Reserve”) declined the requests of plaintiffs-appellants Lori Gardner-Alfred and Jeanette Diaz for a religious exemption from a policy that required all Federal Reserve employees to be fully vaccinated against Covid-19. The Federal Reserve then fired Gardner-Alfred and Diaz when they failed to comply with that vaccination policy. Gardner-Alfred and Diaz sued, claiming that the Federal Reserve’s actions infringed upon their religious liberties in violation of, inter alia, the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, the Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment, and Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. The district court (Lewis J. Liman, J.) granted summary judgment to the Federal Reserve on Gardner-Alfred’s and Diaz’s claims. In addition, the district court found that, while litigating their claims, Gardner-Alfred and Diaz both engaged in discovery misconduct, and on motion of the Federal Reserve, imposed sanctions in the form of adverse inference instructions and an award of attorneys’ fees and expenses occasioned by that misconduct. On appeal, Gardner- Alfred and Diaz challenge the district court’s imposition of discovery sanctions and grant of summary judgment against them. 3 We conclude that the district court did not abuse its discretion by imposing sanctions and that the district court properly granted summary judgment on Gardner-Alfred’s claims. We also conclude, however, that disputed issues of material fact about whether Diaz’s sincerely held religious beliefs conflict with the Federal Reserve’s vaccination policy preclude summary judgment against Diaz. Accordingly, we AFFIRM in part and VACATE in part the judgment of the district court, and REMAND the case for further proceedings. BACKGROUND Gardner-Alfred and Diaz were executive assistants to C-suite officers at the Federal Reserve when the Covid-19 pandemic began. Like many other employers, the Federal Reserve responded to the pandemic by shifting most of its employees, including Gardner-Alfred and Diaz, to remote work starting in March of 2020. That policy continued until, in the summer of 2021, the Federal Reserve announced its intention to begin “a phased return to the office after Labor Day,” which required employees to return to work in person several days a week. App’x 893. As part of that transition, the Federal Reserve adopted a vaccination policy, which provided that “[a]s a condition of employment, every individual 4 employed by the [Federal Reserve] must be fully vaccinated against COVID-19, as defined in applicable public health guidance, and receive a booster shot within thirty (30) days of becoming eligible to do so, unless they receive an accommodation related to this requirement.” Id. 56. As relevant here, employees could apply for an exemption from the policy based on “a sincerely held religious belief that precludes receiving the COVID-19 vaccine” by submitting “a religious accommodation request form” with a “clear[]” explanation as to “why receiving the COVID-19 vaccination would be contrary to their religious beliefs.” Id. 57. Gardner-Alfred and Diaz sought religious exemptions from the vaccination policy on August 9, 2021 and September 1, 2021, respectively. The Federal Reserve granted them both “temporary accommodation[s]” from the vaccination policy until November 30, 2021. Id. 86, 1092. On November 29, however, the Federal Reserve decided not to grant Gardner-Alfred and Diaz permanent religious accommodations, indicated that their temporary accommodations would expire on January 7, 2022, and informed them that they would need to be vaccinated by December 26, 2021 to comply with the vaccination policy. Ultimately, Gardner-Alfred and Diaz did not get vaccinated and, as a result, they were fired on March 14, 2022. 5 I. Procedural History A. Early Stages of the Lawsuit Prior to their termination, Gardner-Alfred and Diaz filed this lawsuit in the Supreme Court of New York, seeking to enjoin the Federal Reserve from firing them for their refusal to comply with the vaccination policy.1 The Federal Reserve timely removed the case to the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York. Gardner-Alfred and Diaz then filed an amended complaint, the operative complaint for purposes of this appeal, alleging that the Federal Reserve’s actions violated the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (“RFRA”), the Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment, Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, New York State’s Human Rights Law, and New York City’s Human Rights Law.
